summaries.example: Imagine seeing a red apple. You might be wrong about whether it is really an apple, or whether it is on the table. Price says your experience still gives you something important: a red, round-looking thing is present to you. He calls such an experienced item a sense-datum. He also says we should not decide too quickly what sense-data are made of. We should follow the evidence.
summaries.summary: Henry Habberley Price was a twentieth-century philosopher who studied how experience helps us think about the world. He was especially interested in perception: what happens when we see or touch things. Price argued that philosophy should pay close attention to what experience actually shows. He also defended common sense as a useful beginning for philosophical questions. However, he did not think every question had an immediate answer. If experience supported the existence of something but did not reveal its deeper nature, he recommended metaphysical neutrality: do not claim more than the evidence allows. Price was an empiricist, meaning that experience plays a central role in understanding ideas and testing beliefs. His work also examined how we recognize things, how beliefs guide action and thought, and how ideas from David Hume can help us understand the external world. The source entry presents Price as a careful and constructive thinker whose influence later became less visible, even though his questions remain important.
key_ideas: Price tried to follow experience wherever it led instead of starting with many fixed ideas.
He thought ordinary experience and common sense are important starting points for philosophy.
He believed experiences can support beliefs about the world without making every belief perfectly certain.
When evidence does not tell us whether something is physical, mental, or something else, we should remain neutral.
Price studied perception, thinking, belief, and the ideas of the philosopher David Hume.
summaries.why_it_matters: Price’s approach teaches a useful habit: look carefully at what you experience, separate strong evidence from guesses, and avoid pretending to know more than you do. This matters whenever people disagree about what they saw, what a belief means, or how much evidence is enough. His work also shows that philosophy can clarify confusing questions instead of merely choosing sides.

important_terms.definition: A philosopher is someone who carefully examines big questions about knowledge, reality, and how we think.
Evidence is information or experience that gives us a reason to accept or question an idea.
Empiricism is the view that experience is very important for understanding ideas and testing beliefs.
Common sense means the ordinary ways people usually think about the world and their experiences.
A sense-datum is an item directly present in an experience, such as a color or shape that you notice.
Metaphysical neutrality means waiting to decide what something really is when the evidence does not settle the question.

questions_to_think_about: Can an experience give you a good reason to believe something without proving it completely?
When should we trust common sense, and when should we investigate further?
If you see something that looks red, what exactly do you know?
Is it better to choose an explanation quickly or wait for more evidence?

summaries.example: Suppose you look at a tomato. You may doubt whether it is really a tomato, whether its color is exactly uniform, or whether an object exists outside your experience. Price argues that at least some feature of the experience—something red and round being present to consciousness—is directly given. He calls this a sense-datum. But he does not infer from that alone whether sense-data are physical objects, mental items, or entities of another kind. The experience supports further beliefs about a tomato, yet those beliefs remain open to error and interpretation.
summaries.summary: Henry Habberley Price developed a broad, experience-centered philosophy. In perception, he argued that careful attention to experience reveals items directly presented to consciousness, which he called sense-data. These data help explain how we form beliefs about material objects, but Price distinguished support from certainty: experience can confirm a claim without making error impossible. He also separated the question of what is given in experience from the metaphysical question of what sense-data ultimately are. They might be physical, mental, or of another kind; where the evidence does not decide, philosophy should remain neutral. Price’s empiricism holds that understanding a concept involves a recognitional capacity: one should be able to identify its application when the appropriate experience occurs. His defense of common sense treats ordinary experience as a necessary starting point for philosophy, since scientific reasoning itself depends on it. In his account of belief, dispositions explain how beliefs guide action, emotion, and further thought. His discussions of Hume similarly explore how experience and imagination support our ordinary conception of a continuing external world, while raising difficult questions about induction and justification.
key_ideas: Price treats experience as philosophically significant evidence, not merely as material to be explained by science.
His empiricism links understanding a concept with being able to recognize when it applies in experience.
He defends common sense because scientific and philosophical reasoning already depend on ordinary experience and thought.
His neutralism is selective: he accepts what the evidence supports, while withholding judgment about unsupported metaphysical interpretations.
His analyses of recognition and belief emphasize capacities and dispositions, not only inner episodes occurring at a single moment.
His work on Hume examines how experience, imagination, and ordinary practices support belief in an external world and induction.
summaries.why_it_matters: Price’s philosophy models disciplined inquiry. It asks us to distinguish what experience directly presents, what it supports, and what a theory adds beyond the evidence. That distinction is useful in debates about perception, skepticism, science, memory, belief, and interpretation. His work also illustrates how a philosopher can develop detailed theories while remaining cautious about conclusions that the evidence does not warrant.

important_terms.definition: Empiricism is the view that concepts and theories must ultimately be connected with experience, including sense experience or introspection.
Phenomenological inquiry examines how experience is presented from the subject’s point of view, rather than only studying its physical causes.
Perceptual acceptance is the mind’s taking something to be present in perception; it may occur even when the perception is mistaken.
A sense-datum is an item directly sensed or presented in experience, whose deeper metaphysical nature may remain unsettled.
The Principle of Confirmability says that a sense-datum can provide initial support for claims about a material object, without guaranteeing them.
Metaphysical neutrality is withholding judgment between competing accounts of what something is when experience does not decide among them.
Recognition is a capacity to identify a characteristic or individual when encountered; it helps explain how concepts operate.
A disposition is a stable capacity or tendency to behave, feel, or think in certain ways under suitable conditions.

questions_to_think_about: Does being unable to doubt a feature of experience show that the feature exists independently of the mind?
Can science criticize common sense without relying on ordinary forms of evidence and reasoning?
Is a theory genuinely neutral if it accepts sense-data but leaves their nature undecided?
Are beliefs best understood as mental occurrences, dispositions, or a combination of both?
Does Price’s empiricism provide a satisfactory way to evaluate religious or other unusual experiences?

summaries.example: Imagine walking around a playground tree. At first you notice separate colors, shapes, and patches of bark. After seeing the tree from several angles, you form a stronger conviction that one three-dimensional object is there, even when part of it is hidden. Price would say your experiences help confirm this belief, but they do not make it impossible that you are mistaken. He also asks what exactly is present in experience and whether those experienced features are physical, mental, or something else. He thinks the evidence may support the question without settling every answer.
summaries.summary: Henry Habberley Price was a British philosopher whose work centered on experience, perception, concepts, belief, and common sense. He held that philosophical inquiry should begin by examining the evidence of experience rather than by imposing a large metaphysical system in advance. His empiricism connects understanding with recognition: to understand an idea is, in part, to know how to identify its application when the relevant experience occurs. Price’s account of perception introduces sense-data, items directly present in sensory experience. These help explain how we arrive at beliefs about material objects, but Price’s Principle of Confirmability makes the support provisional rather than infallible. He also distinguishes phenomenological questions about how perception presents things from scientific questions about the physical causes of perception. Price’s defense of common sense does not mean every ordinary belief is unquestionable. Instead, common sense is the unavoidable platform from which philosophical and scientific criticism begins. His metaphysical neutrality is another form of caution: evidence may establish that something plays a role in experience without settling whether it is physical, mental, or something else. In his theory of belief, dispositions explain how beliefs can guide action, emotion, and reasoning even when no conscious thought is occurring.
key_ideas: Price says philosophy should follow experiential evidence and examine how experience supports belief.
He distinguishes the causes of perception, which science may study, from the character of perception, which philosophical analysis also investigates.
He argues that common sense has authority as a starting point because reasoning and science depend on ordinary experience.
Price accepts that perception can provide evidence for a material world while denying that this evidence gives complete certainty.
His metaphysical neutrality separates claims supported by experience from further claims about the ultimate nature of what is experienced.
His account of belief emphasizes dispositions that can guide behavior, emotions, and later reasoning.
summaries.why_it_matters: Price offers a practical method for handling difficult disagreements. First identify the experience or evidence; then ask what it really supports; finally separate that support from additional assumptions about reality. This method can make debates about perception, science, common sense, and belief clearer. It also shows why philosophical analysis remains valuable even when scientific research explains the causes of an experience.

important_terms.definition: Empiricism is the idea that experience is a major source of knowledge and a test for whether concepts and theories connect with reality.
Phenomenological inquiry studies how things appear in experience, while scientific inquiry often studies the physical causes of those experiences.
A sense-datum is something directly present in a sensory experience, such as a color or shape noticed while seeing an object.
Perceptual acceptance is taking something to be there in perception; it can occur even when the perceived thing is not actually there.
The Principle of Confirmability is Price’s view that experiences give initial evidence for material objects and their features, but not absolute proof.
Common sense is ordinary thought and experience, which Price treats as a starting point rather than an infallible final answer.
Metaphysical neutrality means not choosing between possible accounts of reality when the available evidence cannot decide.
A disposition is a tendency or capacity that can produce thoughts, feelings, or actions in appropriate circumstances.

questions_to_think_about: Why might an experience support a belief without guaranteeing that the belief is true?
What is the difference between studying what causes seeing and studying what seeing is like?
Can common sense be both a useful starting point and something that needs criticism?
If two metaphysical explanations fit the same evidence, should we choose one or remain neutral?
How might a belief affect what someone does, feels, or thinks next?
